meta.intro: A branch of ideas built on top of everything merged so far, run against a made-up house on this computer. Each section is one thing that was built, with what it does, how it was checked, and a screenshot of it running.
meta.how:
Everything here lives on one branch that was never merged or deployed, so your real server, its history and its settings are exactly as you left them. The numbers on the screenshots belong to a made-up house (a simulator with three weeks of generated history), so they are not your electricity. The screenshots are of the real dashboard code, running locally.

Each section says feature (something new), insight (something the data can now tell you), fix (something that was wrong) or finding (something I noticed). If you like a piece, ask for it to be made into a pull request; the commits are small and in order, so pieces can be picked one at a time.

entries.title: A demo house to run all of this on
entries.summary: The simulator now behaves like a believable house instead of a repeating pattern, so every feature below could be shown with realistic data without touching your real server.
details: A garage sub-panel (the EV charger and a workshop inside it) and a desk PC and monitor on the office circuit, next to the circuits it already had.

Each day has its own plan worked out from the date: the car charges on about 70% of nights and tapers off at the end, the dryer runs on some days, the air conditioner works harder on a hot day, the office is quiet at the weekend. The same day always looks the same, and the live readings follow the same plans as the history.

-sim-days 21 writes three weeks of made-up history once; scripts/demo.sh runs everything on its own port with its own temporary database and scripts/demo-seed.py lays it out the way you have yours: nesting, a computer with its collector's CPU, GPU and memory, a group, favorites and a price.
Tests: the history has every meter for every minute, is identical when made twice, never exceeds a meter's cap, and a window can run past midnight.

images.caption: The flow chart over seven days of the demo house: the house, the garage panel holding the EV charger and the workshop, and the desk PC's parts.

entries.title: Runs: every time the car charged or the dryer ran
entries.summary: A meter's page now has a Runs card: each stretch the meter was really working (a charging session, a dryer load, an oven preheat), with how long it lasted, how much energy it took and what it cost. For the EV charger it reads like a charging log: 7 runs, about 21 kWh and $3.36 each, 3 h on average.
details: Why it matters: a bill is a monthly lump; a run is something you can act on. "A charge costs $3.36 and I do it five nights a week" is a number you can compare with the public charger or with moving the charge to the cheap hours.

How a run is found (no new device reading, only the minutes already stored): the level that counts as working is a quarter of the way from the meter's resting power (its 10th percentile) to its working power (its 95th), learned from the last 30 days so that looking at one hour is judged by the same level as a month. A dip of up to five minutes does not end a run (a heating element clicking off), and a stretch shorter than three minutes is not a run. A meter whose busiest and quietest minutes differ by less than 15 W (a router) has no level and no card.

API: GET /api/v1/meters/{id}/runs?from&to with an optional min_watts. It gives the level, the runs newest first (at most 500), each with start, end, minutes, kWh, average and peak watts and a cost, plus totals over all runs and the meter's own energy so the card can say what share of the meter the runs hold. A run is listed in the period it starts in and is followed up to 12 hours past the end so it is whole. The cost is the run's energy at the price of the day it started (the same schedule code every other figure uses; no price saved gives no cost, never a zero).
Phone: on a narrow screen each run becomes two lines (when and cost on the first, the bar and length on the second).

Note for the demo: the simulator plans each day on its own, so a charge that would cross midnight is cut at midnight into two runs ("Fri 12:00 AM" is the tail of Thursday night's charge). A real car would not do this; it is a simulator artefact.

images.caption: The EV charger over seven days: seven charging sessions beside the power chart that shows the same seven plateaus.
The same card at phone width (375 px).

entries.tests: Go: five API tests (charges listed newest first with exact kWh, cost at the day's price, a steady fridge has no runs, a run belongs to the period it starts in and is whole, bad asks are refused), plus the earlier detection tests. Web: runs.test.ts. Contract example meter-runs.json validates against the schema.
entries.notes: Not verified: on your real house (only the simulator's charger was looked at), and with a car that tapers its charge in many small steps (the 5-minute dip rule may split such a charge). A compressor that cycles (a fridge) also gets a Runs card, with many short runs: that is true to what it does but not very useful; the card could be hidden for runs shorter than ten minutes on average.

entries.title: Always on: the power the house never goes below
entries.summary: A new Always on card on the Live page (for the house) and on every meter's page: the power it hardly ever drops below, what a year of that costs, and what share of everything it uses is on all day and night. In the demo house: 460 W, $637 a year, 12% of use.
details: Why it matters: the always-on floor is the part of the bill you pay for doing nothing, and the easiest part to cut (a standby box, an old freezer, a monitor that never sleeps). Seeing it as a yearly dollar figure makes it concrete.

How it is worked out: the 5th percentile of the minute averages over the period picked (not the single lowest minute, so one dropped reading or glitched clamp cannot set it). A year of it is priced at today's price; the share is the floor divided by the average of the same minutes. Under an hour of recorded minutes it says nothing (the endpoint answers 204 and the card is not drawn).
The house is the two mains legs added minute by minute; a minute where one leg is missing is left out, so the sum is never one leg short. Nothing is added to anything else.

"What each meter rests at" (house card only): each meter that holds no other meter, biggest first. They are explicitly not added to each other or to the house's floor, because the quietest minutes of different meters need not coincide; the card says so.

images.caption: The Live page over seven days: the house never goes below 460 W; a year of that is $637. The list beneath shows what each meter rests at.
The same card on the Office circuit's page at phone width.

entries.tests: Go: baseload package tests (what it rests at, one glitched minute does not set it, under an hour says nothing, negative and broken readings are not power, a meter that uses nothing has no share) and API tests (a meter's floor, its yearly cost at the saved price with no cost when no price is saved, the house floor never one leg short, the breakdown lists only meters that hold nothing, 204/404/400 cases). Web: baseload.test.ts. Contract example validates.
entries.notes: Finding in the demo: the house floor (460 W) is much larger than any meter's own floor (the biggest is 40 W), because the simulator has about 300 W of unmetered base load. On a real house that gap (the floor of the house minus the floors of what is metered) would say how much always-on power no clamp sees; I did not turn it into a number, because floors of different meters are not additive. A cycling appliance (the fridge) rests at its off level between cycles, so its floor reads as 4 W rather than its average; the card says so. Not verified on your real house.
